question:
A cluster of five servers communicates only by message passing over an asynchronous network, with no bound on message delay or relative processing speed. The operators guarantee that no server will ever crash, so the failure model allows zero crash failures. Messages are eventually delivered. The servers must agree on a single value.
Does the Fischer-Lynch-Paterson (FLP) impossibility result imply that these servers cannot achieve agreement? (Yes/No)
atom_statement: The Fischer-Lynch-Paterson (FLP) result says that agreement cannot be achieved in an asynchronous message-passing system if even one crash failure is allowed.
evidence: The Fischer-Lynch-Paterson (FLP) result [FLP85] says something much stronger: you can’t do agreement in an asynchronous message-passing system if even one crash failure is allowed.1 After its initial publication, it was quickly generalized to other models including asynchronous shared memory [LAA87], and indeed the presentation of the result in [Lyn96, §12.2] is given for shared- memory ﬁrst, with the original result appearing in [Lyn96, §17.2.3] as a corollary of the ability of message passing to simulate shared memory.

options.A: If the proposer does not change often, the accept! and accepted messages can be skipped between consecutive instances, leaving a single round-trip per operation.
options.B: If the proposer does not change often, the prepare and ack messages can be skipped between consecutive instances, leaving a single round-trip per operation.
options.C: If the proposer changes frequently, the prepare and ack messages can be skipped between consecutive instances, leaving a single round-trip per operation.
options.D: If the proposer does not change often, the prepare and ack messages can be skipped between consecutive instances, leaving two round-trips per operation.

question:
In multi-Paxos, an optimization reduces the cost of certifying consecutive operations. Which statement correctly gives the condition under which it applies, the messages that can be skipped between agreement instances, and the resulting per-operation cost?
A) If the proposer does not change often, the accept! and accepted messages can be skipped between consecutive instances, leaving a single round-trip per operation.
B) If the proposer does not change often, the prepare and ack messages can be skipped between consecutive instances, leaving a single round-trip per operation.
C) If the proposer changes frequently, the prepare and ack messages can be skipped between consecutive instances, leaving a single round-trip per operation.
D) If the proposer does not change often, the prepare and ack messages can be skipped between consecutive instances, leaving two round-trips per operation.
atom_statement: In multi-Paxos, if the proposer does not change often, the prepare and ack messages between agreement instances for consecutive operations can be skipped, reducing the time to certify each operation to a single round-trip of accept! and accepted messages.
evidence: If the proposer doesn’t change very often, a further optimization allows skipping the prepare and ack messages in between agreement protocols for consecutive operations.
This reduces the time to certify each operation to a single round-trip for the accept! and accepted messages, which is about the best we can reasonably hope for.

key_points: There is a reachable state q_0, a split of the n processes into two nonempty teams A_0 and A_1, and an operation assigned to each process
After any execution in which each process applies at most one of its assigned operations, each process can tell which team the first operation came from
Formally, for each process j, the sets of (response, final state) pairs for executions starting with team A_0 and with team A_1 are disjoint
question: What does it mean for a readable object type T to be n-discerning?
atom_statement: A readable object type T is n-discerning if there exist a reachable state $q_0$, a split of processes $p_1,\dots,p_n$ into two nonempty teams $A_0$ and $A_1$, and an operation $\pi_i$ assigned to each $p_i$, such that $R_{A_0,j}\cap R_{A_1,j}=\emptyset$ for every process id $j$, where $R_{A_b,j}$ is the set of pairs $\langle r,q\rangle$ for which some execution $q_0\pi_{i_1},\dots,\pi_{i_k}$ has all $i_\ell$ distinct, includes $p_j$, has $p_{i_1}\in A_b$, has $p_j$'s operation return $r$, and ends with the object in state $q$; this means that after any such sequence of operations each process can tell whether the first operation was performed by a process in team $A_0$ or team $A_1$.
evidence: A readable object type T is n-discerning if it has a reachable state q0 in which it is possible to split processes p1, . . . , pn into two nonempty teams A0 and A1 and assign each process pi an operation πi, so that after any sequence of operations πi1, . . . , πik, each process can tell if the ﬁrst operation πi1 was performed by a process in team A0 or team A1.11 To formalize this, let us deﬁne RAb,j for each b ∈{0, 1} and each process id j as the set of all pairs ⟨r, q⟩for which there is an execution q0πi1, . . . , πik where (a) all the iℓare distinct; (b) one of them is pj, (c) pi1 ∈Ab, (d) pj’s operation returns r, and (e) the ﬁnal state of the object is q.
Then T is n-discerning if, there exist a state q0, teams A0 and A1, and operations π1, . . . , πn, such that RA0,j ∩RA1,j = ∅for all j.

key_points: T is n-discerning (the equivalence holds in both directions)
question: For a readable object type T, what property of T is equivalent to T having consensus number at least n in the $h^r_m$ hierarchy?
atom_statement: For any readable object type T, $h^r_m(T)\ge n$ if and only if T is n-discerning.
evidence: For any readable object T, hrm(T) ≥n if and only if T is n-discerning.

question:
True or False?
"Whether the $h^r_m$ hierarchy of consensus numbers is robust for arbitrary deterministic objects is still an unresolved question."
atom_statement: It is an open question whether the $h^r_m$ hierarchy of consensus numbers is robust for arbitrary deterministic objects.
evidence: Whether or not the resulting hierarchy is in fact robust for arbitrary de- terministic objects is still open, but Ruppert [Rup00] subsequently showed that it is robust for RMW registers and objects with a read operation that returns the current state, and there is a paper by Borowsky, Gafni, and Afek [BGA94] that sketches a proof based on a topological characterization of computability3 that hrm is robust for deterministic objects that don’t discriminate between processes (unlike, say, single-writer registers).

key_points: Only crash failures, with f < n/2
question: Under what system-model assumptions (timing, network, and failures) can shared-memory registers be implemented on top of message passing, as in the ABD register simulation?
atom_statement: Shared memory can be implemented from message passing in a system that is asynchronous, has a complete network, and has only f < n/2 crash failures.
evidence: Here we show how to implement shared memory from message passing.
We’ll assume that our system is asynchronous, that the network is complete, and that we are only dealing with f < n/2 crash failures.

question:
A designer implements a replicated read/write register over message passing among n = 5 processes. Each process keeps a local state consisting of two fields: a stored data value and an integer tag. The tag is raised with each newer write, and no maximum value is imposed on it, so it can grow without limit.
Does this local state (a value paired with an unbounded integer timestamp) match the stored state used in the ABD register simulation? (Yes/No)
atom_statement: In the ABD register simulation, the stored state is a pair (value, timestamp), where timestamps are unbounded integer values.
evidence: will hold a pair (value, timestamp) where timestamps are (unbounded) integer values.

question:
In a message-passing register simulation of the ABD kind with n = 5 processes, every process starts the execution holding the pair consisting of an undefined placeholder value (⊥) and timestamp 0, before any read or write is invoked.
Is this initial configuration the one used in the ABD register simulation? (Yes/No)
atom_statement: In the ABD register simulation, everybody initially starts with the pair (⊥, 0).
evidence: Initially, everybody starts with (⊥, 0).

question:
A team designs a failure detector for an asynchronous crash-prone system. Its specification guarantees that, after some unknown time, at least one correct process is never suspected by any correct process. However, the detector is known not to be strongly complete: it only guarantees weak completeness.
Does this failure detector belong to the class of eventually strong failure detectors (◇S)? (Yes/No)
atom_statement: An eventually strong failure detector (class ◇S) is strongly complete and eventually weakly accurate.
evidence: ♦S (eventually strong) Strongly complete and eventually weakly accu- rate.

question:
A team runs an asynchronous system with crash failures. Every process has a failure detector module of class ◇P (eventually perfect). A protocol they want to deploy needs failure detectors of class S. They hope to write one general reduction algorithm that uses only the ◇P outputs and the ordinary message exchange to emulate a detector of class S at every process.
Can class ◇P simulate class S, so that such a general reduction is guaranteed to exist? (Yes/No)
atom_statement: In the structure of failure detector classes, the class ♦P cannot simulate the class S.
evidence: What is trickier is to show that this structure doesn’t collapse: ♦P can’t simulate S, S can’t simulate ♦P, and ♦S can’t simulate any of the other classes.

Can class S simulate class ◇P, so that such a general reduction is guaranteed to exist? (Yes/No)

evidence: What is trickier is to show that this structure doesn’t collapse: ♦P can’t simulate S, S can’t simulate ♦P, and ♦S can’t simulate any of the other classes.

question:
A shared-memory system has four processes, each with its own single-writer register. Processes P2, P3 and P4 crash permanently at arbitrary points, some in the middle of their own operations. The surviving process P1 still completes every snapshot and every write it starts, in a finite number of its own steps. It never waits for any other process to take a step, and this holds in every execution.
Does this protocol exhibit the wait-free property for atomic snapshots? (Yes/No)
atom_statement: A wait-free atomic snapshot protocol is one in which any process can finish its own snapshot or write even if all the other processes lock up.
evidence: But it gets harder if we want a protocol that is wait-free, where any process can ﬁnish its own snapshot or write even if all the others lock up.

question:
A system has eight shared registers and no process ever crashes. A scanning process acquires a lock covering the entire register file, so all writers are blocked. It reads all eight registers one by one, and then releases the lock so the waiting writers can proceed.
Does the vector of values read by the scanner form an atomic snapshot of the registers? (Yes/No)
atom_statement: Without failures, an atomic snapshot is easy to obtain by locking the whole register file, reading all the registers, and unlocking them to let the starving writers in.
evidence: This is easy without failures: we simply lock the whole register ﬁle, read them all, and unlock them to let all the starving writers in.

question:
In a snapshot implementation, each process's register holds a value together with an embedded snapshot taken at the time of its write. A scanner repeatedly collects all registers. The collects never match one another. Across successive collects, the scanner sees three different values from process P2. It stops and returns the snapshot embedded in the second of P2's writes that it observed.
Is this way of finishing the snapshot a direct scan? (Yes/No)
atom_statement: A snapshot operation repeatedly performs collects, and if it gets two identical collects it can return the results of those collects; this is called a direct scan.
evidence: So a snapshot repeatedly does collects until either (a) it gets two identical collects, in which case it can return the results (a direct scan, or (b) it sees three diﬀerent values from the same process, in which case it can take the snapshot collected by the second write (an indirect scan).

question:
In a snapshot implementation, a scanner repeatedly collects all registers. Its latest two consecutive collects return exactly the same values in every register. The scanner returns those values as its snapshot. It does not use any snapshot embedded in another process's write.
Is this way of finishing the snapshot an indirect scan? (Yes/No)
atom_statement: A snapshot operation that repeatedly performs collects and sees three different values from the same process can take the snapshot collected by the second of that process's writes; this is called an indirect scan.
evidence: So a snapshot repeatedly does collects until either (a) it gets two identical collects, in which case it can return the results (a direct scan, or (b) it sees three diﬀerent values from the same process, in which case it can take the snapshot collected by the second write (an indirect scan).

question:
A shared read/write register initially holds 0. In the concurrent execution $H$, process $p$ invokes write(1) and then crashes, so it never receives a response. After that invocation, process $q$ invokes read, and this read responds with value 0. No other events occur. Consider the sequential execution $S$ that contains only $q$'s read operation returning 0.
Is $S$ a linearization of the incomplete execution $H$? (Yes/No)
atom_statement: A linearization of a possibly incomplete concurrent execution $H$ is built in three steps: - Extend $H$ with zero or more response events to get $H'$. - Remove the invoke events in $H'$ that have no matching response to get $H''$. - Construct a sequential execution $S$ that meets the object's sequential specification, with $H''|p = S|p$ for all processes $p$ and $<_{H''} \subseteq <_S$.
evidence: implementation the ﬂexibility of deciding whether these operations have taken eﬀect or not, so given an incomplete concurrent execution H, a linearization of H involves three steps:
Extend H by adding zero or more response events, obtaining a new execution H′.
Remove any invoke events in H′ that don’t have a matching response event, obtaining a new execution H′′.
Construct a sequential S such that S meets the sequential speciﬁcation of the object, H′′|p = S|p for all p, and <H′′⊆<S.2

question:
True or False?
"In exponential information gathering, each process does a lot of gossiping, and its state is just a flat set of inputs, with no record of who it heard each value from."
atom_statement: In exponential information gathering, each process does a lot of gossiping, and its state is a tree describing who it heard what from rather than a flat set of inputs.
evidence: The idea of exponential information gathering is that each process will do a lot of gossiping, but now its state is no longer just a ﬂat set of inputs, but a tree describing who it heard what from.

key_points: At most $f$ processes are faulty, so at least one of those nodes is good (non-faulty)
question: In the agreement argument for exponential information gathering (EIG), why does every path in the tree contain at least one node whose value is common to all correct processes?
atom_statement: In the exponential information gathering (EIG) agreement argument, every path in the tree has a common node on it, because a path travels through $f+1$ nodes and one of them is good.
evidence: Agreement: Observe that every path has a common node on it, since a path travels through f +1 nodes and one of them is good.

question:
True or False?
"When exponential information gathering is used in the Byzantine failure model, a message from process j that is missing or ill-formed is replaced by a default value, and the rest of the data-collecting part proceeds as in the crash failure model."
atom_statement: When exponential information gathering (EIG) is applied in the Byzantine model, ill-formed or missing messages from a process j are replaced by default values, and otherwise the data-collecting part of EIG proceeds as in the crash failure model.
evidence: To apply EIG in the Byzantine model, ill-formed or missing messages from j are replaced by default values, but otherwise the data-collecting part of EIG proceeds as in the crash failure model.

question:
A shared-memory protocol for 3 processes is to be run by simulators using the BG simulation. In the protocol, each simulated process repeats the same two-step pattern: it takes a snapshot of the shared array, then performs an update that writes a value computed from that snapshot and its own local state. No simulated process ever performs two updates in a row or two snapshots in a row.
Does this protocol have the structural form that the BG simulation relies on, so that the simulators can determine a simulated process's actions just by determining the sequence of snapshots it receives? (Yes/No)
atom_statement: The BG simulation assumes that all simulated processes alternate between taking snapshots and doing updates, so that the actions of a simulated process can be determined by determining the sequence of snapshots it receives.
evidence: To avoid having to simulate speciﬁc choices of operations, the BG simulation assumes that all simulated processes alternate between taking snapshots and doing updates.
This approach means that we can determine the actions of some simulated process by determining the sequence of snapshots that it receives.

question:
A BG-style simulation uses one safe agreement object per (simulated process, step) pair. A modified simulator i is allowed to begin proposing to the safe agreement objects of two different simulated processes, j and k, before finishing either. It then crashes while still inside the unsafe interval (between starting and finishing its proposal) of both objects. No other simulator crashes.
Is it guaranteed that the crash of simulator i stalls at most one safe agreement object? (Yes/No)
atom_statement: Because each simulating process is in the unsafe interval of at most one safe agreement object at a time, the crash of a simulating process can stall at most one safe agreement object and hence knocks out at most one simulated process.
evidence: The termination property of Sjr means that this can only occur if the failure occurs while i is in the unsafe interval for Sjr—but since i is only in the unsafe interval for at most one Sjr at a time, this stalls only one simulated process j.
It follows that each failure of a simulating process knocks out at most one simulated process.
